title: Datalist, Output, and Progress Elements
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of datalist, output, and progress elements in a browser document.
Apply at least one relevant rule from this lesson to a small HTML example.
Check the result using browser inspection, a validator, or an accessibility checklist.

content.intro: This lesson turns “Datalist, Output, and Progress Elements” into a practical authoring skill. You will work with the <datalist> element, understand the choices that matter, and check the result instead of relying on guesswork.
content.why_it_matters: Tables and forms carry structured data. Semantic relationships and understandable constraints improve both usability and the reliability of information sent to an application.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Datalist provides suggestions associated with an input; suggestions are not a strict validation rule.

items.title: The <datalist> element
items.text: Datalist provides suggestions associated with an input; suggestions are not a strict validation rule.

items.title: Suggestion lists for input controls
items.text: Form controls need meaningful labels and names, clear instructions, and constraints that match the data. Treat browser validation as feedback for users, not proof that submitted data is trustworthy.

items.title: The <output> element
items.text: Output represents the result of a calculation or user action.

items.title: The <progress> element
items.text: Progress represents completion progress toward a task goal.

items.title: The <meter> element
items.text: Meter represents a scalar measurement within a known range; it is not task progress.

items.title: Representing progress, quantities, and measurements semantically
items.text: Representing progress, quantities, and measurements semantically is one of the decisions covered by Datalist, Output, and Progress Elements. Decide what the markup is meant to communicate, choose the native HTML structure that expresses that meaning, and verify the result in a browser or a relevant validation checklist. Avoid using an element or attribute just because its default appearance seems convenient.

content.task: Create a small HTML example that demonstrates datalist, output, and progress elements. Keep the markup minimal, give every element a clear purpose, and inspect the rendered result.
task_acceptance_criteria: Use the relevant concept from Datalist, Output, and Progress Elements.
Keep IDs unique and use valid nesting.
Check the result in a browser and record one finding.

Compare the source and rendered DOM if the behavior surprises you.

troubleshooting.symptom: The expected content does not appear.
troubleshooting.check: Confirm the file was saved with an .html extension and inspect its path and nesting.
Check the resolved URL and confirm the referenced file or external resource exists and allows the request.

troubleshooting.symptom: The page looks correct but the markup may be invalid.
troubleshooting.check: Run the Nu Html Checker and follow its first relevant diagnostic, then validate again.

common_mistakes.why: The default appearance is not the element’s main meaning and can make navigation or maintenance harder.
common_mistakes.fix: Choose the element that matches the content purpose, then use CSS for presentation.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a browser’s recovery means the source is valid
common_mistakes.why: Browsers often recover from malformed markup, which can hide defects and produce unexpected document structure.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect the rendered DOM and run a validator against the original source.

common_mistakes.why: Missing files, narrow viewports, keyboard access, invalid input, or other states can expose defects.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the expected state plus one realistic edge case and an accessibility path.

Verify both markup and behavior; do not infer correctness from appearance alone.
